description: We’re a motivated team of developers and AI enthusiasts participating in NASA Space Apps for the first time. Our current team includes Frontend/React, Backend, AI/ML, and Flutter skills, and we’re excited to build a creative, practical solution using NASA data.
summary:
VitalTrace — Astronaut Health Self-Assessment Twin

On a crewed Mars mission, astronauts are up to 20 minutes from Earth by radio, one way. With no doctor on board and no answer from Houston in under 40 minutes, VitalTrace helps an astronaut understand what is happening inside their own body, and what to do about it, right now.

It is built around a "body twin": nine body systems (heart, brain, eyes, inner ear, lungs, bones, kidneys, metabolism, immune system), each with a live risk score. Tap any organ to trace the cause chain: space hazard, organ, indicator, countermeasure.

A daily check-in logs blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, and mood, then returns a readiness score and triage: handle it yourself, involve the crew medical officer, or queue a report for Earth. A threat simulator previews the effect of a solar storm, sleep loss, or less exercise, and a mission planner turns findings into daily protocols.

Thresholds and trends are grounded in NASA Human Research Program knowledge (five hazards, bone loss, radiation limits, communication delay), and every modeled number is labeled. It runs entirely in the browser on a simulated 160-day Mars mission dataset, with no setup.

Deep-space crews will be their own first responders. VitalTrace turns scattered physiology data into one story: hazard, organ, evidence, action.
details:
VitalTrace: Astronaut Health Twin — Team Out of_Orbit
Live prototype: https://vitaltracee-1ci8.vercel.app
What it does
On a Mars mission, a message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes, so astronauts must assess their own health. VitalTrace is an onboard health twin that turns daily readings into an explained decision. It uses one chain, Hazard → Organ → Metric → Action, based on NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. Every number shows what it means, why space caused it, and what to do now.
Main use
Each morning the astronaut logs heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, SpO₂, sleep, water, exercise, mood and symptoms in about 60 seconds. VitalTrace updates a clickable body twin of nine systems. Each system gets a 0–100 risk score, a status (Nominal, Caution or Critical) and the person who must act: the astronaut, the crew medical officer or the flight surgeon on Earth.
How it works
Each reading is scored against mission thresholds. The scores combine into body-system risk, and symptoms add to the system they affect. Values are compared with the astronaut’s own baseline, which is the average of their first 60 days. A 7-day trend predicts how many days are left before a system reaches the red zone. Four destination profiles (Space Station, Deep Space Transit, Moon, Mars) change the radiation dose, exercise targets and signal delay. Simulators test decisions before acting, and a one-page report is ready for the flight surgeon. Everything runs in the browser with no Earth link.
Data
Thresholds and rates come from published sources:
- NASA HRP hazards and risks
- NASA-STD-3001 (600 mSv career limit and the 95% bone-density floor)
- NASA bone-loss rates
- Curiosity RAD radiation measurements
- Clinical guidelines for blood pressure, glucose and sleep
The demo uses a synthetic 160-sol crew record built from these ranges. Every value is labeled MEASURED, PREDICTED, SIMULATED or NASA-INFORMED.
Working now
- Body twin with triage and responders
- Daily check-in with “How to measure” guides, red-flag symptoms and an Earth report queue
- Cabin sensors linked to body systems
- Trend charts and early warnings
- What-if and threat simulators
- Countermeasure planner and the flight-surgeon report
Limitations
- All data is synthetic, and the tool is not a medical device or a diagnosis.
- It follows one astronaut, and no real sensors are connected.
- Data is not saved between visits.
- The baseline is shown but does not yet change the score.
Future plans
- Image input (reading a value from a photo of a device)
- A sources panel behind the NASA-INFORMED labels
- Personal-drift scoring
- A crew view for the medical officer
- Real wearables
- Validation with analogue-mission data
Benefits and goal
Astronauts get a fast answer to “Am I OK, and what do I do?”. The medical officer sees what needs review today, and the flight surgeon gets a short report instead of raw data. It needs no new hardware, and the same approach could help people far from doctors on Earth. Our goal is more independent, safer crews on deep-space missions.
Tools
- TypeScript, React, TanStack Router, Vite and Tailwind CSS
- Recharts
- Built with Lovable and hosted on Vercel
- Runs in any web browser, with no special hardware
dataRefs: The 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight (NASA HRP) We use this as the overall framework of the app: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity (or its absence), and closed/hostile environments. NASA explains that these hazards interact and amplify each other's effects on the body, which is why we built a "What-if" simulator that shows how changing one factor affects several indicators at once.

Risks of Human Spaceflight (NASA HRP) We derived our health indicators from this page. Every indicator in the app is linked to a risk listed here, such as bone loss, cardiovascular changes, immune function, nutrition, sleep, and behavioral and psychological changes. The page also notes that the impact of these risks varies depending on the mission destination, which is the basis for the differences between our mission environments.
Ongoing HRP Research in Space (NASA) A reference showing that research on astronaut health is still underway. We use it to connect our indicators to current research.
projectRefs: Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health (CSA) We use it to justify our cumulative radiation dose indicator, and to show that neutron radiation accounts for roughly 30% of radiation on the International Space Station and that instruments exist to measure radiation continuously, which supports the idea of self-monitoring.

Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space? (CSA) We use it to explain why studying human health in the space environment matters, and how the results benefit future exploration and life on Earth.
